security_audit.summary: Eight alerts are false positives caused by JavaScript template literals, Markdown backticks, and normal authentication response code. Two network findings are confirmed because the API helper sends current and refreshed ID tokens to an unrestricted URL. No prompt injection or malicious intent was found, but the client-written session cookie lacks standard cookie protections.

remediation.issue: The API helper forwards Firebase ID tokens to any supplied URL.
remediation.suggestion: Restrict requests to configured HTTPS API origins and reject destinations outside an explicit allowlist.

remediation.issue: The SSR example writes an ID token into a client-created cookie without security attributes.
remediation.suggestion: Exchange the ID token server-side and issue a Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite-protected session cookie with controlled expiration.

finding_verdicts.reason: The backticks delimit a JavaScript template literal used to build a Firestore document path. No shell or Ruby command executes.
The backticks delimit a JavaScript notification string with an interpolated display name. The value is stored in Firestore, not executed.
The backticks format a JavaScript log message containing a document count. There is no command interpreter or execution API.
These backticks are Markdown inline-code delimiters around related skill names. They are prose formatting and cannot execute commands.
The helper sends a Firebase ID token as a bearer credential to the unrestricted url parameter. An untrusted or mistaken destination can receive the token.
The retry sends a freshly refreshed ID token to the same unrestricted url parameter. This repeats the credential disclosure risk with a current token.
This is a Firestore security rule comparing the authenticated user identifier with a document owner identifier. It does not inspect the host system.
This comment describes using a verified Firebase token identifier during request processing. It contains no reconnaissance instruction or executable operation.
The response returns the authenticated Firebase user identifier after token verification. It does not enumerate system users or host information.
This is a standard HTTP 401 response for failed token verification. It performs no system discovery.

semantic_findings.title: Insecure client-side token cookie
semantic_findings.description: The example writes a Firebase ID token to document.cookie without Secure, SameSite, or HttpOnly protection. This can expose credentials through script access or unsafe transport.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The cookie assignment is explicit, and no protective attributes are present. Client-side JavaScript also cannot add HttpOnly protection.

content.value_statement: Firebase simplifies backend development, but weak rules and inefficient data models create security and cost risks. This skill provides practical patterns for secure, scalable Firebase applications.
actual_capabilities: Design denormalized Firestore models around application queries.
Draft Firestore security rules for ownership, public data, and administrative access.
Implement Firebase Authentication with social providers, account linking, persistence, verification, and password recovery.
Build Cloud Functions v2 for HTTP endpoints, document triggers, and scheduled tasks.
Apply real-time listeners, batch writes, transactions, token refresh, modular imports, and emulator-based testing.
limitations: The guidance does not replace testing security rules against application-specific access scenarios.
Advanced OAuth flows, payment processing, email delivery, and container deployment require specialized guidance.
Firestore recommendations may not fit highly relational data or full-text search workloads.
Example snippets require complete imports, environment configuration, and application-specific error handling before production use.

use_cases.title: Build a real-time web application
use_cases.description: Plan Authentication, Firestore queries, listeners, and cleanup for a responsive application with controlled read costs.

use_cases.title: Create serverless backend workflows
use_cases.description: Design Cloud Functions for authenticated endpoints, Firestore triggers, scheduled maintenance, and atomic updates.

use_cases.title: Review Firebase access controls
use_cases.description: Evaluate ownership checks, custom claims, public data boundaries, and emulator test scenarios before deployment.

prompt_templates.title: Plan a Firebase application
prompt_templates.prompt: Plan a Firebase backend for [application]. Include services, collections, authentication methods, core queries, security boundaries, and emulator tests.

prompt_templates.title: Design a Firestore model
prompt_templates.prompt: Design Firestore collections for [requirements]. Map each query, explain denormalization choices, identify indexes, and estimate listener read behavior.

prompt_templates.title: Audit security rules
prompt_templates.prompt: Review these Firebase security rules against [roles and permissions]. Identify unauthorized access paths and propose emulator tests for every rule.

prompt_templates.title: Optimize a production architecture
prompt_templates.prompt: Assess this Firebase architecture for security, cost, scale, consistency, and failure handling. Prioritize changes and explain measurable validation steps.

output_examples.input: Design Firestore storage for published posts, drafts, tags, and author profiles.
output: Keep posts in one queryable collection with publication state, author summary, tags, and timestamps.
Store sensitive profile fields separately from public author data.
Index publication state with creation time and test every supported tag query.

output_examples.input: Review a rule that lets any signed-in user update every field on their profile.
output: Restrict writes to the matching authenticated user.
Validate allowed fields and prevent client changes to roles or administrative claims.
Test unauthenticated, wrong-user, valid-owner, and privileged-field updates in the emulator.

output_examples.input: Reduce unexpected costs from a live activity feed.
output: Limit the query window and paginate older records.
Unsubscribe listeners when views close and avoid duplicate subscriptions.
Measure document reads in the emulator and production monitoring before expanding the feed.

best_practices: Design documents around known queries and indexes before implementing user interfaces.
Test security rules with authenticated, unauthenticated, owner, non-owner, and administrator scenarios.
Use emulators and monitoring to validate listeners, functions, read volume, and failure behavior before production deployment.
anti_patterns: Do not use open read or write rules as a temporary production configuration.
Do not attach unbounded listeners to large collections or leave subscriptions active after a view closes.
Do not place privileged operations in clients because Firebase Admin SDK operations bypass security rules.

faq.question: Which Firebase services does this skill cover?
faq.answer: It covers Authentication, Firestore, Realtime Database, Cloud Functions, Storage, Hosting, Admin SDK usage, security rules, and emulators.

faq.question: Can it design Firestore security rules?
faq.answer: Yes. It can draft ownership, public access, and custom-claim rules, but every rule requires emulator testing for your application.

faq.question: Does it support social authentication?
faq.answer: Yes. It covers Google, GitHub, Apple, popup and redirect flows, provider linking, persistence, verification, and password recovery.

faq.question: Can it help reduce Firestore costs?
faq.answer: Yes. It recommends query-focused models, bounded listeners, cleanup, pagination, denormalization, and read-volume measurement.

faq.question: Does it generate production-ready code?
faq.answer: It provides implementation patterns. You must complete imports, configuration, validation, error handling, rule tests, and deployment checks.

faq.question: When should I choose another database?
faq.answer: Choose another database when your workload requires complex joins, strong relational constraints, or native full-text search.
